title: Norovirus Reference Information
question: According to the *Bad Bug Book*, what is the estimated infective dose of norovirus, when do symptoms usually begin, what are the characteristic symptoms, and how can food workers contaminate ready-to-eat food?
final_result:
- Infective dose: the Bad Bug Book (2012 FDA pathogen reference, not a regulation) states the norovirus infective dose is very low, estimated to be as low as 1 to 10 viral particles, while viral particles are excreted at high levels by both symptomatic and asymptomatic people (as high as 1 x 10^12 viral particles per gram of feces). [bad-bug-book:p169:c0]
- Onset: a mild, brief illness usually develops between 24 and 48 hours after consuming contaminated food or water (median in outbreaks 33 to 36 hours), with onset times within 12 hours of exposure reported; the consumer snapshot likewise says symptoms usually start within 1 or 2 days but may start in as few as 12 hours. [bad-bug-book:p169:c0; bad-bug-book:p168:c2]
- Characteristic symptoms: acute-onset vomiting (often explosive), watery non-bloody diarrhea with abdominal cramps, and nausea; explosive, projectile vomiting is usually the first sign of illness and is often used to characterize the illness, and headache, low-grade fever, chills, and muscle aches may also occur. [bad-bug-book:p169:c1]
- Course of illness: symptoms generally persist for 12 to 60 hours (mean 24 to 48 hours), with most people feeling better within 1 to 2 days; dehydration is the most common complication, especially among the very young, the elderly, and those with underlying medical conditions. [bad-bug-book:p169:c2]
- Food-worker contamination of ready-to-eat food: foodborne norovirus illnesses are epidemiologically linked to consumption of ready-to-eat (RTE) foods contaminated by food workers (along with environmental contamination of produce and contaminated molluscan shellfish), with transmission occurring through the fecal-oral route (or vomit on occasion) and often associated with improper sanitation controls or their application. [bad-bug-book:p170:c0; bad-bug-book:p170:c1]
- Any ready-to-eat food handled by ill food workers may be contaminated; salad ingredients, fruit, and oysters are the foods most often implicated, and nearly 29% of all norovirus foodborne outbreaks from 1997-2004 were attributed to food purchased or served at a restaurant or delicatessen. [bad-bug-book:p170:c1]
- Contamination can occur without visible illness: about 30% of infected people show no gastrointestinal illness or symptoms yet still excrete high levels of virus in stool ("silent shedders"), and the virus may continue to pass in bowel movements even after symptoms resolve; alcohol-based antibacterial hand gels do not protect against norovirus, so handwashing is especially important. [bad-bug-book:p169:c2; bad-bug-book:p168:c3]

claims.text: Infective dose: the Bad Bug Book (2012 FDA pathogen reference, not a regulation) states the norovirus infective dose is very low, estimated to be as low as 1 to 10 viral particles, while viral particles are excreted at high levels by both symptomatic and asymptomatic people (as high as 1 x 10^12 viral particles per gram of feces).

Onset: a mild, brief illness usually develops between 24 and 48 hours after consuming contaminated food or water (median in outbreaks 33 to 36 hours), with onset times within 12 hours of exposure reported; the consumer snapshot likewise says symptoms usually start within 1 or 2 days but may start in as few as 12 hours.

Characteristic symptoms: acute-onset vomiting (often explosive), watery non-bloody diarrhea with abdominal cramps, and nausea; explosive, projectile vomiting is usually the first sign of illness and is often used to characterize the illness, and headache, low-grade fever, chills, and muscle aches may also occur.

Course of illness: symptoms generally persist for 12 to 60 hours (mean 24 to 48 hours), with most people feeling better within 1 to 2 days; dehydration is the most common complication, especially among the very young, the elderly, and those with underlying medical conditions.

Food-worker contamination of ready-to-eat food: foodborne norovirus illnesses are epidemiologically linked to consumption of ready-to-eat (RTE) foods contaminated by food workers (along with environmental contamination of produce and contaminated molluscan shellfish), with transmission occurring through the fecal-oral route (or vomit on occasion) and often associated with improper sanitation controls or their application.

Any ready-to-eat food handled by ill food workers may be contaminated; salad ingredients, fruit, and oysters are the foods most often implicated, and nearly 29% of all norovirus foodborne outbreaks from 1997-2004 were attributed to food purchased or served at a restaurant or delicatessen.

Contamination can occur without visible illness: about 30% of infected people show no gastrointestinal illness or symptoms yet still excrete high levels of virus in stool ("silent shedders"), and the virus may continue to pass in bowel movements even after symptoms resolve; alcohol-based antibacterial hand gels do not protect against norovirus, so handwashing is especially important.

You also play a part in the safety of what you eat. When you read the consumer boxes, you’ll see that
different pathogens can be risky in different ways, and that a safety step that’s effective against one
might not be as effective against another. So what should you do? The answer is to follow some simple
steps that, together, lower the risk from most pathogens.
 Washing your hands before and after handling food, and in between handling different foods, is one
of the most important steps you can take. Do the same with equipment, utensils, and countertops.
 Wash raw fruits and vegetables under running water. These nutritious foods usually are safe, as you
probably know from the many times you’ve eaten them, but wash them just in case they’ve
somehow become contaminated. For the most part, the less of a pathogen on a food – if any – the
less chance that it can make you sick.
 Cooking food to proper temperatures kills most bacteria, including Salmonella, Listeria, and the
kinds of E. coli that cause illness, and parasites.

Common names of the illness, which is the leading cause of foodborne illness in the United
States, are viral gastroenteritis, acute nonbacterial gastroenteritis, food poisoning, and winter
vomiting disease.
 Mortality: Overall, these illne sses account for 26% of hospitalizations and 11% of
deaths associated with food consumption.
 Infective dose: The infective dose is very low; it is estimated to be as low as 1 to 10
viral particles, and the particles are excreted at high levels by both symptomatic and
asymptomatic people (as high as 1 x 1012 million viral particles/g feces).
 Onset: A mild, brief illness usually develops between 24 and 48 hours after contaminated
food or water is consumed (median in outbreaks: 33 to 36 hours), but onset times within
12 hours of exposure have been reported.

 Illness / complications: Norovirus illness is self-limiting, but can be very debilitating as
a result of the high rate of vomiting. Recovery is usually complete and without evidence
of long-term effects. Dehydration is the most common complication, especially among
the very young, the elderly, and patients with underlying medical conditions.
No specific therapy exists for viral gastroenteritis, in general, or NoV infection, in
particular. For most people, treatment of NoV infection is supportive; besides rest, it
consists primarily of oral rehydration and, if needed, intravenous replacement of
electrolytes. Currently no antiviral medication is available, and antibiotics are not
effective for treating NoV infection. Presently no vaccines are available to prevent NoV
infection, although this is an active area of research.
 Symptoms: Symptoms usually present as acute-onset vomiting (often explosive);
watery, non-bloody diarrhea with abdominal cramps; and nausea. Explosive, projectile
vomiting usually is the first sign of illness and is often used to characterize the illness.
Headache, low-grade fever, chills, and muscle aches may also occur. The severity of

vomiting usually is the first sign of illness and is often used to characterize the illness.
Headache, low-grade fever, chills, and muscle aches may also occur. The severity of
symptoms appears to be higher in hospitalized patients, immunocompromised people,
and elderly people, compared with younger adults and other groups.
Studies suggest that 30% of people infected with NoV display no gastrointestinal illness
or associated symptoms, but still excrete high levels of virus in their stool. These distinct
groups of people are considered to be silent shedders of NoV.
 Duration: Symptoms generally persist for 12 to 60 hours, with a mean period of 24 to 48
hours. Most people report feeling better within 1 to 2 days. However, for hospitalized
patients, immunocompromised people, and the elderly, vomiting and diarrhea generally
resolve within 72 to 96 hours, while the non-specific symptoms, such as headache, thirst,
and vertigo, could persist up to 19 days.
